question_html: What is a Bank Pass Book primarily defined as?

options.A: A copy of the customer's account in the books of the bank
options.B: A ledger maintained by the business enterprise for cash transactions
options.C: A statement of all assets and liabilities of the bank
options.D: A summary of the cash sales made by the enterprise

answer_html: Answer: (A) Bank pass book is merely a copy of the customer's account in the books of a bank[cite: 13].

question_html: A debit balance in the depositor's Cash Book corresponds to which of the following in the Bank Statement / Pass Book?
answer_html: Answer: (B) The debit balance in the cash book represents credit balance in the pass book because the business enterprise treats the bank as a debtor and the bank treats the business as a creditor[cite: 13].

question_html: What is the primary purpose of preparing a Bank Reconciliation Statement?

options.A: To rectify all errors in the general ledger
options.B: To reconcile the difference between the bank balance shown by the cash book and the bank passbook
options.C: To calculate the net profit of the business

answer_html: Answer: (B) A bank reconciliation statement is mainly prepared to reconcile the difference between the bank balance shown by the cash book and bank passbook[cite: 13].

question_html: Which of the following documents are compared to prepare a Bank Reconciliation Statement?

options.A: Bank statement and cash column of the Cash Book
options.B: Bank statement and bank column of the Cash Book
options.C: Cash column and bank column of the Cash Book

answer_html: Answer: (B) A Bank Reconciliation Statement is prepared with the help of the bank statement and the bank column of the Cash Book[cite: 13].

question_html: When the balance as per the Cash Book is the starting point, how are direct deposits by customers into the bank treated?
answer_html: Answer: (A) When the balance as per Cash Book is the starting point, direct deposits by customers increase the pass book balance, hence they are added[cite: 13].

question_html: When the balance as per Pass Book is the starting point, how is interest allowed by the bank treated?
answer_html: Answer: (B) When balance as per Pass Book is the starting point, interest allowed by bank is subtracted to arrive at cash book balance[cite: 13].

question_html: Which of the following is considered a timing difference in bank reconciliation?

options.A: Cheques issued but not yet presented for payment
options.B: Wrong casting of the cash book
options.C: A cheque recorded twice in the cash book
options.D: Bank charges debited by the bank

answer_html: Answer: (A) Cheques issued but not yet presented represent a timing difference between the cash book and pass book entry[cite: 13].

question_html: Why is regular bank reconciliation considered an important internal control tool?

options.A: It helps in detecting errors, frauds, and discourages embezzlement of funds
options.B: It automatically posts journal entries to ledger accounts
options.C: It determines the exact income tax liability of the firm
options.D: It replaces the need for an annual audit

answer_html: Answer: (A) Regular reconciliation acts as an internal control tool that brings out errors, undue clearance delays, and discourages embezzlement[cite: 13].

question_html: In how many formats can a Bank Reconciliation Statement generally be prepared?

options.B: Two formats ('Balance' presentation and 'Plus & Minus' presentation)

answer_html: Answer: (B) Bank Reconciliation Statement can be prepared in two formats: 'Balance' presentation and 'Plus & Minus' presentation[cite: 13].

question_html: When should the cash book be adjusted before preparing the Bank Reconciliation Statement at the end of the financial year?

options.A: Mandatorily, to reflect correct bank balance in the balance sheet
options.C: Only if the bank instructs so
options.D: Only when there are no timing differences

answer_html: Answer: (A) Adjusting the cash book at the end of the financial year is necessary so as to reflect the correct bank balance in the balance sheet[cite: 13].

question_html: The cash book showed an overdraft of ₹1,50,000, but the pass book showed that cheques of ₹10,000, ₹5,000, and ₹12,500 respectively had not been presented for payment; and a cheque of ₹4,000 paid into account had not been cleared. What is the balance as per the pass book?
answer_html: Answer: (C) Starting with overdraft as per cash book (-1,50,000): Add unpresented cheques (+10,000 + 5,000 + 12,500 = +27,500); Less uncleared deposits (-4,000). Total = $-1,50,000 + 27,500 - 4,000 = -1,26,500$ (i.e. overdraft/Dr balance as per pass book of ₹1,26,500)[cite: 13].
topic_text: Practical Calculation of Pass Book Balance

question_html: When drawing up a Bank Reconciliation Statement starting with a debit balance as per the Bank Statement (overdraft as per pass book), how should cheques issued but unpresented be treated?
answer_html: Answer: (B) Starting with a debit balance as per Bank Statement (overdraft), unpresented cheques are deducted to arrive at cash book balance[cite: 13].

question_html:
When drawing up a BRS starting with a debit balance as per Bank Statement, which of the following items are added?

1. Cheques issued but not presented to bank
2. Bills Receivable collected directly by bank
3. Overcasting of the debit side of bank account in the cash book
answer_html: Answer: (C) As per standard BRS rules table starting from unfavourable balance (Dr.) of pass book, unpresented cheques, B/R collected directly, and overcasting of debit side of cash book are all added[cite: 13].

question_html: A cheque for ₹25,000 that was issued and presented for payment in the same month was erroneously recorded on the debit side of the cash book (instead of credit). What difference will this cause when comparing with the pass book?
answer_html: Answer: (B) Recording a payment as a receipt (debit instead of credit) requires a double adjustment (once to nullify the wrong debit and once to record the actual credit), causing a difference of ₹50,000[cite: 13].

question_html: A cheque of ₹80,000 discounted from the bank was dishonoured, and the bank charged ₹1,600 as charges on account of the same. While starting with a debit balance in the cash book for preparing BRS, what amount needs to be deducted?
answer_html: Answer: (C) Both the dishonoured cheque (₹80,000) and bank charges (₹1,600) debited by the bank reduce the pass book balance, meaning a total of ₹81,600 must be deducted when reconciling from cash book balance[cite: 13].

question_html: If the payment side of the cash book is undercast, how does it affect the cash book balance and what is its treatment in BRS when starting from cash book balance?

options.A: Cash book balance is overstated; added in BRS
options.B: Cash book balance is understated; subtracted in BRS
options.C: Cash book balance is overstated; subtracted in BRS
options.D: No effect on cash book balance

answer_html: Answer: (C) Undercasting of the payment side means fewer payments are recorded, overstating the cash book bank balance. To reconcile, it must be subtracted[cite: 13].

question_html: When a customer receives a cash discount of 5% on an account of ₹2,000 and pays by cheque, but the cashier erroneously enters the gross amount in the bank column of the cash book, what is the adjustment required in the cash book?

options.A: Reduce cash book bank balance by ₹100
options.B: Increase cash book bank balance by ₹100
options.C: Reduce cash book bank balance by ₹2,000

answer_html: Answer: (A) The net amount received is $2,000 - (5% of 2,000) = ₹1,900. Recording the gross amount (₹2,000) overstates the cash book bank balance by ₹100, which must be deducted[cite: 13].
topic_text: Discount Recording Errors in Cash Book

question_html: A bill receivable for ₹1,530 discounted for ₹1,500 with the bank had been dishonoured on 30th March, but advice was received on 1st April. If books are closed on 31st March without an adjusted cash book, how is this treated in the BRS starting from cash book balance?

options.A: Deducted because the bank debited the full amount (including charges/face value)

answer_html: Answer: (A) Dishonour of discounted bill means bank debits customer's account for the full face value/amount, which is not yet recorded in the cash book, hence deducted when starting from cash book balance[cite: 13].

question_html: If an opening debit balance of ₹2,156 in the cash book was brought forward as a credit balance on the previous day, what adjustment is required in the cash book or BRS?

options.A: An adjustment of ₹4,312 to correct the wrong sign/side

answer_html: Answer: (A) Bringing forward a debit balance as a credit balance understates the cash book balance by $2,156 \times 2 = \text{₹}4,312$ (removing the wrong credit and providing the correct debit)[cite: 13].

question_html: A cheque issued amounting to ₹1,725 was returned marked 'out of date'. No entry was made in the cash book. How should this be treated when adjusting the cash book?

options.A: Credited to Cash Book (to reverse the payment entry since the cheque is stale/out of date)
options.C: Ignored in Cash Book and put only in BRS

answer_html: Answer: (A) When a cheque becomes out of date (stale), the earlier payment entry must be reversed by crediting the bank column in the cash book[cite: 13].
